notes: The whole 45-page PDF, read end to end: the preface, the Gilded Age historic context, and the five style themes (Italianate/Flat-Front Italianate, Stick/Eastlake, Queen Anne, Second Empire, Richardsonian Romanesque), each with its narrative, evaluative framework, eligibility standards, character-defining features, integrity considerations and figures, plus the bibliography. There is no inventory table and no APN anywhere in the document: every address comes from a figure caption or from the narrative and property-type descriptions that name known examples of a style. The dense seam is the figure captions, which give an address, a style, a landmark number and a year.

coverage.remaining: None. The document was read in full; nothing in it is outstanding.
coverage.note: 45 numbered-address mentions across 45 pages, resolving to 42 distinct addresses plus one block face with no street number (the east side of Harrison Street between 21st and 22nd, Olsen's Queen Anne Cottages). Three of the mentions sit inside citations to other documents — a footnote naming the ordinance that designated 22 Beaver Street, a figure source credit naming the 90-92 Second Street landmark designation report, and a bibliography entry for the National Register nomination of the house at 584 Page Street — and are recorded at low confidence because they are not claims this statement makes. Four of the printed addresses are rows of separate houses rather than one building's two-number address (1104-1118 Tennessee, 725-733 Castro, 905-911 Minnesota, 710-718 Steiner); each is recorded as the two numbers the document actually prints, one finding apiece.

findings.description: The Audiffred Building, San Francisco Landmark No. 7, built in 1889 — the only known commercial example of the Second Empire style in San Francisco, and one of the few local buildings in the style built of masonry rather than wood. Three storeys, with a mansard roof carrying pedimented dormers, quoining, a corbelled cornice line and arched window surrounds.

findings.description: The San Francisco Gas Light Company building, San Francisco Landmark No. 58, built in 1893 — one of the few known Richardsonian Romanesque buildings in the city, and judged individually significant for its round tower with a conical roof, corbelled cornice, arched window surrounds and Syrian arch at the entry. A two-storey industrial building, now in commercial use.

findings.description: The Sharon Building in Golden Gate Park, San Francisco Landmark No. 124, built in 1888 as a canteen for women and children and now a community art centre. One of the few known Richardsonian Romanesque buildings in the city and the only local example with rough-hewn stone wall surfaces, it is judged individually significant for that stonework, its cross-gabled form, round-arched windows and arched entry.

citation.label: Anne Greening and Elena Moore, San Francisco Planning Department, Victorian Era Styles (1870-1910) Historic Context Statement, SF Survey Cultural Resources Survey, adopted 2022
citation.locator: p. 38 and p. 41 (narrative); p. 39, Fig. 38; p. 43, Fig. 42

raw.text: Sharon Building, 300 Bowling Green Drive, Golden Gate Park, 1888, San Francisco Landmark No. 124. This park structure has rough-hewn stone wall surfaces, which are common for the style but not found in other San Francisco examples.

resolution.method: EAS exact match on 300 BOWLING GREEN DR → parcel 1700001; sf-parcels has blklot 1700001 active, 1101–1199 09TH; the 2025 roll records it as miscellaneous/mixed-use. The assessor files the parcel as 1750 OAK ST. EAS puts 10, 50, 300, 320 BOWLING GREEN DR on that parcel, so per the directory contract the fact belongs on one page at the lowest, 10. The parcel is all 4,195,976 sq ft of Golden Gate Park, so there is no building-level page for the Sharon Building and the fact goes on the park's own page. That page already carries facts about individual structures inside the park — Kezar Pavilion, the Beach Chalet, the police academy — from the new-deal-context-statement pass, so this follows the precedent rather than setting one.

findings.description: A four-storey building put up in 1909 as a stable and then an automobile garage, and one of the few known examples of Richardsonian Romanesque architecture in the city — round arches over the entry and one garage opening, a corbelled cornice and banded windows. Built after the style's period of significance, and its brick painted since, it contributes to the local commercial district.
